title: "The Tree Persona (provisional)"

::: {.callout-info appearance="simple"}
**Provisional background.** This working material supports the persona appendices and may change as the research develops.
:::

The Melbourne tree persona should be plural. It should not speak as "the tree" in general, because the evidence splits trees by origin, age, body structure, hydrology, recruitment, fungal relations, governance status, and public conflict.

The strongest working division is:

- **Introduced civic elders**: English elms, London planes, oaks, poplars, ashes, figs and other planted exotics. They provide canopy, heritage, shade, cavities, and sometimes habitat platforms, but carry pest, disease, monoculture, suckering, root, risk, allergy/litter, and replacement tensions.
- **Indigenous eucalypt/wattle systems**: River Red Gum, Yellow Box, Grey Box, Yellow Gum, Manna Gum, Swamp Gum, Blackwood and other wattles. They are not simply "native replacements"; they are hydrological, woodland, bark, nectar, hollow, deadwood, soil, and recruitment systems.
- **Non-local Australian native allies**: Corymbia, Lophostemon, Tristaniopsis, Melaleuca, Ficus, Grevillea, Brachychiton, Flindersia, Casuarina and others. They may be climate-adapted or useful for birds and shade, but should not be equated with local indigenous restoration.
- **Large old trees as a cross-cutting class**: provenance matters, but age/size/decay also matters. Mature trees produce disproportionate canopy, hollows, dead branches, deadwood, bark, roosts, shade, memory, and public attachment.
- **Constrained juveniles**: young street trees in pits, medians, car-park conversions and narrow verges. These are future canopy only if soil, water, protection, and maintenance persist long enough.
- **Spontaneous and unwanted vegetation**: suckers, weeds, vacant-lot trees, verge plants, and emergent urban forests. These are not automatically good or bad. They are latent ecological capacity, management burden, aesthetic conflict, and sometimes genuine habitat.

## Shared characteristics of Melbourne's trees

- **Extreme longevity and slow time-horizons**: a large tree experiences the world across centuries, far beyond the span of any human project that manages it. River Red Gum (*Eucalyptus camaldulensis*) and Yellow Box (*Eucalyptus melliodora*) on Melbourne's volcanic plains persist for many hundreds of years and hold the memory of fires, droughts, and floods that predate the city.[^banks1997][^sillett2015]
- **Modular bodies**: trees live through bodies that are modular rather than singular. A tree can lose a branch, hollow, resprout, compartmentalise decay, and remain alive. For old trees, damage is not only injury; it can become cavity, bark complexity, deadwood, moisture pocket, fungal substrate, perch, roost, nest site, or litter source. Branches die, dormant and adventitious buds activate, and an old trunk can become hollow while the living cambial skin remains functional.[^thomas2014]
- **Sessility and lifelong site-fidelity**: a tree cannot move, so it commits to one place for life and shapes that place rather than leaving it. It must reach every resource it needs, water, light, nutrients, and partners, by growing, which makes soil volume, compaction, and the surrounding community decisive.[^roudavski2021][^stokes2002]
- **Decay generates habitat**: the features that make an old tree valuable to other beings appear only as it ages and partly dies. Hollows, rot holes, cracks, coarse deadwood, and loose bark are products of decay, and cavity occurrence is far higher in large decaying and dead trees than in young healthy ones.[^ibarra2020] Humans read this ageing as disease and remove the snags, logs, and litter that follow, which strips the habitat.[^roudavski2021]. Hollows form through branch breakage, pruning, fungal decay, insects, termites, fire, and time. For fauna they are shelter; for trees they are also internal reorganisation. Hollow elms and other temperate trees can grow adventitious roots into decaying internal wood, effectively recycling nutrients from their own hollow centres.[^thomas2014]
- **Keystone structures**: large trees supply resources, shelter, and structure for many other species. In Canberra parks, large native trees showed a strong positive relationship with five measures of bird diversity, an effect that increased as the trees grew larger and that continued for years after a tree's own death.[^stagoll2012][^lindenmayer2012]
- **Below-ground sociality**: trees acquire nutrients and water through mycorrhizal exchange,  but also live with decay fungi, vascular pathogens, and root rot. Some fungal networks can link neighbouring plants and transfer carbon, nutrients, water, or defence signals. An old tree lives inside a web of fungal threads that link it to neighbours and exchange carbon, nutrients, and defence signals.
- **Hollows take centuries**: in eucalypts, hollows typically begin to form between 120 and 220 years of age, and cavities enlarge with trunk diameter, so the biggest oldest stems carry the most.[^bennett1994][^leroux2014] About 15 per cent of Australia's terrestrial vertebrates, including 114 bird species and 83 mammal species, depend on hollows.[^adkins2006]
- **A mixed native and introduced cohort**: Melbourne's large-tree population is unusually split between indigenous eucalypts and imported European trees. In the City of Melbourne, *Eucalyptus* makes up about 24 per cent of trees, *Ulmus* 13 per cent, and *Platanus* 12 per cent, and elms and planes each make up roughly 10 per cent of the whole.[^melbourne2011diversity] The avenue of about 400 English elms (*Ulmus procera*) along Royal Parade, planted in 1913 and heritage-listed since 2009, is the iconic example.[^roudavski2021]
- **Reproduction tied to disturbance, and easily blocked**: woodland eucalypts cast huge seed crops and recruit into loamy gaps and ash beds opened by fire or flood.[^deccw2011] On sealed, compacted urban ground this recruitment fails, so many street trees cannot replace themselves and depend on humans to plant their successors.[^leroux2014][^roudavski2021]
- **Water is a capability condition**: canopy cooling, photosynthesis, nutrient uptake, hydraulic safety, and survival all depend on water access. Melbourne's drought and water restrictions triggered irreversible decline in many trees, including significant elms.[^melbourne2012strategy]

## How  trees live in the city now

- **Sealed, compacted soil**: pavement seals the ground so rain cannot infiltrate, and compaction collapses the pore spaces root tips need. Restricted root-penetrable soil volume becomes a main limit on long-term access to water and nutrients.[^mullaney2015][^jim2023]
- **Short urban lives**: street trees average about 13 years in highly urban cores against about 37 years one street back in residential areas, and planted cohorts show annual mortality of roughly 4 to 7 per cent, highest in the first five years.[^mullaney2015][^hilbert2019]
- **Simplified and removed before ageing**: intensive maintenance keeps trees small and simplifies their structure, and managers remove most trees long before the hollows and deadwood of old age can form.[^grossmann2020][^hilbert2019]
- **Urban old growth exists but is interrupted**: old-growth conditions genuinely occur in cities, redefined relative to the most recent regional forest-resetting event. Loeb documents examples across 28 countries and 62 metropolitan areas, including Australian entries, but notes that many urban old-growth forests can no longer reproduce because human modification breaks historical continuity.[^loeb2011]
- **Composition is set by supply as much as ecology**: nurseries and homeowners choose much of what grows, so urban forests often concentrate around a small set of genera and ornamental preferences rather than local ecosystem processes.[^avolio2018]
- **Sapling counts can hide old-tree loss**: mature tree loss above about 1 per cent per year makes canopy targets difficult to achieve, and around or above 3 per cent per year generally performs poorly. A young tree cannot speak as a replacement for an old tree without acknowledging the decades of missing canopy, hollows, deadwood, and relationships.[^croeser2025]
- **Regeneration pathways.** Tree reproduction in cities ranges from seedling recruitment to clonal suckering, epicormic shoots, coppicing, nursery propagation and direct planting. English elm rarely sets seed and is highly effective in vegetative propagation; River Red Gum recruits through see
- **Deadwood and fallen limbs.** Deadwood is a tree-derived resource island, not just waste. Larger and older coarse woody debris supports stronger increases in microbial, invertebrate, plant, nutrient and soil-function responses than smaller or younger debris. Fallen branches and coarse woody debris are also part of senescent eucalypt woodland function, not simply failures of maintenance.[^killey2010][^mallen2026] Retaining natural deadwood matters because introduced or artificially created deadwood can support life but may follow different fungal and nutrient trajectories from naturally aged wood.[^wetherbee2022][^pyne2024][^lasota2018]
- **Severed or mismatched fungal connections**. [^gorzelak2015] In old-growth stands the largest oldest trees act as the most connected hubs, and young saplings establish within their network.[^beiler2010] Sealing and sterilising urban soil severs these partnerships.[^stevenson2020]. The fungal networks can differ between trees. For example, elms are associated with arbuscular mycorrhizal families, while eucalypts can form both ectomycorrhizal and arbuscular associations.[^thomas2014][^stevenson2020][^gorzelak2015] .This means not every urban tree can simply plug into the same network.[^thomas2014][^stevenson2020][^gorzelak2015][^beiler2010][^teste2020]

## Shared use of place and resources

All of Melbourne's large trees, native and introduced alike, build their lives and the lives of dependent beings out of the same set of structures, which a single tree generates in sequence as it grows, ages, and decays. Each structure supports particular tree capabilities, Acquire Resources, Communicate, and Reproduce, and many become the exact habitat the Bird and Lizard personas need.

**Root zone and soil volume.** For a tree, the ground is not a flat surface but a volume of possible root life. Roots require space, oxygen, water, mineral nutrients, fungal partners, and tolerable bulk density. Sealed pavements reduce water infiltration and gas exchange; compacted soils restrict root growth; restricted root volumes create water stress and predispose trees to pest and disease problems.[^melbourne2011diversity][^mullaney2015][^jim2023]

**Water pathways.** Trees use rainfall, stormwater, irrigation, shallow soil moisture, groundwater, and sometimes flood recession. City design changes whether water runs past a tree into drains or enters the root zone. In Melbourne, water sensitive urban design, porous paving, structural soil, suspended pavement, kerb inlets, parking-lane conversions and stormwater capture are not only human infrastructure; they are tree habitat.[^melbourne2012strategy][^page2015][^tirpak2019][^croeser2022]

**Light and canopy room.** Trees acquire energy through leaves, so canopy exposure, shading by buildings, pruning clearances, powerline corridors, street width, and competition with other trees directly condition their life. Large deciduous elms and planes were historically valued because they provided summer shade while allowing winter light.[^royal-parade][^melbourne2011diversity]

**Fungal and microbial partners.** Mycorrhizal fungi extend the effective resource-gathering capacity of roots, trading soil nutrients and water for plant carbon. Physical fungal networks can link multiple trees, and some studies show possible nutrient or defence-signal transfer.[^beiler2010][^gorzelak2015][^karst2023][^henriksson2023] Fungi also return tree bodies to soil through saprotrophic decomposition. Urban disturbance, imported soil, compaction, pollution, trenching, sealed pavement and low organic matter can simplify or redirect these relations.[^thomas2014][^stevenson2020][^dighton2016][^grassi2023][^barber2013]

**Chemical signalling and defence.** Trees respond to injury, drought, herbivory, pathogens, and neighbouring organisms through internal signalling, defensive compounds, tyloses, gums, compartmentalisation, root exudates, and volatile compounds. In elms, ring-porous wood and Dutch elm disease make water-conducting vessels a critical vulnerability: the pathogen blocks the vascular system, while the tree's own defensive blockage can also interrupt water movement.[^thomas2014]

**Regeneration pathways.** Tree reproduction in cities ranges from seedling recruitment to clonal suckering, epicormic shoots, coppicing, nursery propagation and direct planting. English elm rarely sets seed and is highly effective in vegetative propagation; River Red Gum recruits through seed, floodwater dispersal, moist seedbeds, and survival of seedlings until roots reach deeper water.[^gil2004][^distefano2002]

**Wounds, hollows and internal decay.** Hollows form through branch breakage, pruning, fungal decay, insects, termites, fire, and time. For fauna they are shelter; for trees they are also internal reorganisation. Hollow elms and other temperate trees can grow adventitious roots into decaying internal wood, effectively recycling nutrients from their own hollow centres.[^thomas2014]

**Deadwood and fallen limbs.** Deadwood is a tree-derived resource island, not just waste. Larger and older coarse woody debris supports stronger increases in microbial, invertebrate, plant, nutrient and soil-function responses than smaller or younger debris. Fallen branches and coarse woody debris are also part of senescent eucalypt woodland function, not simply failures of maintenance.[^killey2010][^mallen2026] Retaining natural deadwood matters because introduced or artificially created deadwood can support life but may follow different fungal and nutrient trajectories from naturally aged wood.[^wetherbee2022][^pyne2024][^lasota2018],

**Bark, leaf litter and epiphytes.** Bark texture, peeling bark, fissures, retained litter, moss, lichens, epiphytes, mistletoe and canopy humus create surfaces and nutrient cycles. In Melbourne streetscapes, epiphytes can be rare but possible: one study found an epiphytic moss in fissured bark of a non-native oak, indicating that bark structure can matter even on introduced street trees.[^floyed2012]

**Mistletoe and aerial parasitism.** For the host tree, mistletoe is a water and carbon relation that can be stressful at high loads. For urban biodiversity, it can add nectar, fruit, dense foliage, litter nutrients, insect habitat and canopy microclimate. Melbourne's mistletoe reintroduction on London planes shows a direct way to make exotic trees host native aerial plant relations.[^watson2023]

**Human maintenance as habitat pressure.** Pruning, risk works, removal, mowing, herbicide, pavement repair, drain works, possum management, pest treatment and public complaints determine whether branches, hollows, suckers, deadwood and seedlings persist. Maintenance does not only "manage" habitat; it often is the dominant disturbance regime. In veteran-tree management, the crucial design move is often to manage targets, access and expectations around an old tree, rather than to make the tree young, clean or structurally simple again.[^read2000][^lonsdale2013][^fay2002][^ntsg2024][^klein2019]

**The recruitment niche, loamy gaps, and seedfall.** A tree expresses Reproduce by casting seed into ground where seedlings can establish. Woodland eucalypts recruit into loamy gaps and ash beds after fire, so bare, friable, open soil is the limiting resource for the next generation.[^deccw2011] Decaying old trees return nutrients to that soil and nurse the saplings around them, so saplings and dead trees coexist rather than compete.[^roudavski2021] Where management seals the ground, this capability collapses, and the scarcity of saplings beneath large hollow-bearing trees already threatens the supply of future habitat trees.[^leroux2014]

**Spontaneous vegetation and vacant land.** Spontaneous vegetation is plants colonising without planting; the same capacity that crosses a continent can occupy a pavement crack.[^robinson2012] When Blois banned herbicide, plants self-recruited to up to full cover, with 307 species across 48 km and sandy or permeable pavements carrying far more cover than asphalt.[^bonthoux2019] The binding constraint was bare-soil availability and management, not seed supply; weeding frequency had only marginal effect on cover.[^bonthoux2019] In Halifax, spontaneous vegetation patches had higher plant species density than lawns or semi-natural forest and carried pollinator guilds that the other sampled habitats did not.[^robinson2012] Vacant lots are also an underexplored ecological and social resource, and New York City's vacant parcels are often omitted from green-space surveys despite their potential.[^anderson2017] Calling species "weeds" can render self-organising habitats invisible and erasable, and redevelopment of "wastelands" into manicured landscapes can cut existing services.[^pinedapinto2023][^filibeck2016]

## Relationships

**With fungi and soil biota.** Fungi are both partnership and threat.


Fungi are both partnership and threat.

**Beneficial or generative roles:**

- mycorrhizal fungi extend root access to nutrients and water;
- fungal hyphae help bind soil particles and shape soil structure;
- mycorrhizal networks can link plants where continuous soil allows, although strong network evidence is mostly non-urban and should not be overextended to sealed Melbourne streets;
- deadwood fungi decompose lignocellulose, drive decay succession, and help create hollows and saproxylic habitat.

**Risk roles:**

- Dutch elm disease and elm bark beetle vector systems threaten elm avenues;
- Phytophthora-type risks, plane diseases, and other pathogens appear in local tree-management sources;
- taxonomic concentration can magnify pest/pathogen effects.

Which fungi a tree can recruit depends on its mycorrhizal type, and the two main guilds rarely interconnect: elms and most broadleaved exotics are arbuscular (AM), while eucalypts, oaks, willows and poplars are ectomycorrhizal (EM) or dual, so a Melbourne elm and a neighbouring gum partner different fungi and cannot share one network.[^teste2020][^bainard2011][^stevenson2020]

- Much of the eucalypts' EM diversity is hypogeous, fruiting underground as truffles that cannot travel on the wind and depending on digging mammals such as potoroos and bettongs, whose foraging spikes after fire, to spread viable spores, a loop largely absent from the city.[^maser2008][^johnson1995]

- Introduced trees still build networks, though impoverished ones, and planted eucalypts overseas partner mostly novel local fungi rather than co-introduced Australian species, so an exotic can recruit a regional fungal community even where its own is missing.[^authier2022]. [is there anythign on elm trees building fungal networks in cities, and in melbourne or other places where they are nonnative>?] [^santolamazza2019] Sealed surfaces, compaction, salt and low organic matter thin all of this, while large old trees stay the best-connected hubs and the most plausible local inoculum.[^gorzelak2015][^beiler2010] Shared mycelium can carry carbon, nutrients and defence signals, but claims of ubiquitous networks, reliable seedling benefit and offspring-feeding mother trees are unsupported or contested, so state the relation as exchange and association, not intentional communication.[^karst2023]

**Species nuance:**

- *Ulmus* evidence supports AM association at the family level, but local elm mycorrhizal surveys were not found.
- *Eucalyptus* can form ectomycorrhizal associations and may have dual or sequential EM/AM modes.
- *Acacia* nitrogen fixation is bacterial root-nodule work, not fungal, but belongs in the broader soil-partner frame.

**Further risk:**  stevenson-2020:75: "non-native plants in urban landscapes can harbor non-native fungi that may replace native species, causing imbalances in urban ecosystems" (Lothamer et al. 2014; Nuñez & Dickie 2014).

**with Common Mycorrhizal Networks (CMNs)**

The Common Mycorrhizal Networks (CMNs) has been questioned (Karst et al. 2023 — your [^karst2023]), but counters with studies showing benefits (Klein et al. 2023, "facts not fantasy"; Ullah et al. 2024).

What a CMN is claimed to do (the functional definition the paper uses): "facilitate the transfer of water, nutrients and signals between plants," with specific cited benefits — carbon transfer between trees (Klein et al. 2023) and positive effects on plant growth, survival, and community structure (Ullah et al. 2024). Its evidential basis is Beiler et al. 2009, where Rhizopogon fungi were shown to "link multiple Douglas-fir cohorts."

Design implication: protect and repair soil continuity through decompaction, larger rootable volumes, mulch/litter return, stormwater infiltration, construction controls, and deadwood retention.

**Design implication.** Protect and repair soil continuity through decompaction, larger rootable volumes, mulch and litter return, stormwater infiltration, construction controls, and deadwood retention.

**With animals.** Large old trees are keystone structures, with bird richness, abundance and breeding all rising with trunk diameter.[^stagoll2012] Introduced trees contribute when structurally complex, though hollow evidence is strongest for large old trees in general rather than elms in particular. Native mistletoe is a key canopy relation, with an inner-Melbourne *Muellerina eucalyptoides* trial established on London planes and *Ulmus* a plausible host, though Melbourne elm trials were not found.[^watson2023]

**With humans.** Relations are multiple and conflicting: arborists prune, cable, remove, retain and defend; residents complain about roots, litter, risk and views yet also write to trees, mourn them and water them through droughts; developers damage trees through access and trenching; councils count canopy and set diversity targets; and heritage protection preserves form and memory, sometimes against ecological transition.

- **Contested affection**: the premise that everyone loves trees is unstable. When Poland briefly liberalised private tree-felling rules in 2017, landowners removed about 8,000 trees, most on private land, forcing the law to be tightened again.[^kronenberg2021]
- **Risk perception and assessment**: death by tree in public space is rare, but assessors' ratings can shift with assumptions about occupancy and financial loss. Risk work is therefore also a social and institutional practice, not only a property of the tree.[^klein2019]
- **Private-land pressure**: Melbourne professionals report that private landholders often exaggerate tree risk, that education is a key retention lever, and that local protections are weakened by exemptions, enforcement gaps, and low penalties.[^clark2020]
- **Development pressure**: the City of Melbourne removed 19,739 council trees between 2008 and 2017; about 2,000 public street trees were lost within 10 m of major private developments, with removals peaking before completion during groundworks.[^croeser2020]
- **Canopy maths**: mature-tree removal rate correlates strongly and negatively with canopy gain. Targets need removal held near 1 per cent per year and become very difficult above 3 per cent, while observed rates can run higher.[^croeser2025]
- **Care and attachment**: in Fairfield, Melbourne, residents described love for trees, planted memorial trees, and sometimes watered neighbours' trees during drought so council would not remove them.[^pearce2015]
- **Public preferences are selective**: park visitors rated trees that block city views as less important than shade, long lifespan, and wildlife habitat, which shows that tree value is negotiated through particular benefits, inconveniences, and settings.[^jennings2016]

- **Deadwood and property price**: in Kraków, coarse woody debris occurred on 46 per cent of plots but mostly as dead branches in living crowns. Standing dead trees were rare and fallen logs absent, which Fröhlich and Ciach interpret as a management signal: logs and dead trees are usually removed for safety, access, tidiness, and aesthetics.[^frohlich2020]
- **Deadwood and maintenance intensity**: coarse woody debris probability declined as property prices increased, especially in forest remnants and private gardens, probably because wealthier owners or districts can spend more on pruning and deadwood removal. Forest remnants had the most coarse woody debris; urban parks and small green patches were more actively groomed.[^frohlich2020]
- **Veteran-tree microhabitats**: a veteran tree's decaying trunk, loose bark, sap runs, cavities, fungal bodies, and dead branches shelter insects, fungi, lichens, and epiphytes. Habitat features generally appear only after long ageing, often 100 to 200 years or more, so habitat value is a function of time as much as species.[^jim2023][^jonsell2004]
- **Old park trees as biodiversity refuges**: a baroque park built around a 1684 small-leaved lime (*Tilia cordata*) avenue held 18 red-listed beetle species, only slightly fewer than a nearby old-oak forest, including species dependent on a lime-associated fungus.[^jonsell2004]
- **Urban woodpecker and dead-branch habitat**: in Kraków, eight woodpecker species occurred across the city and standing dead branches on living crowns predicted woodpecker richness; gardens and remnants were more important than groomed municipal greenery.[^frohlich2020]
- **Epiphytes on introduced bark**: a survey of 88 Victorian industrial streetscapes found 36 bryophyte species, with the only epiphytic moss growing on a single exotic white oak (*Quercus alba*), indicating that stable bark structure can matter even on introduced street trees.[^floyed2012]

## Native and introduced

- **The heritage paradox**: the city keeps climatically mismatched exotic trees on its grandest avenues while clearing indigenous trees from the country where they belong, and Melbourne's elm stock survives only because the Dutch elm disease that erased it elsewhere never crossed quarantine.[^caudullo2016][^yau1982]
- **Time asymmetry**: an English oak (*Quercus robur*) bears hollows only at 200 to 300 years and under 1 per cent do so before 100, so an exotic tree on a removal schedule cannot be replaced on a human timetable.[^ranius2009]
- **Removal has a real cost**: a radio-tracked Powerful Owl (*Ninox strenua*) in Melbourne day-roosted in exotic trees on all but one occasion, 66.7 per cent of the time, so fast wide clearing of weed trees strips habitat that wildlife actively uses, and removal should be staged.[^mcnabb2011]
- **The exotic-heavy mix is demand-driven**: nurseries and homeowners set composition, not ecology, so the city's reliance on a handful of European genera is a supply choice that can be changed.[^avolio2018][^yarra2017]

## Evidence-based ways to improve tree habitat in modified ecosystems and cities

The studies below show that the habitat value of large trees in cities depends on letting trees grow, age, decay, and collapse across full lifecycles, on retaining the dead wood and cavities that take centuries to form, and on managing human risk through spatial design rather than removal. Each theme runs as an ambition gradient from current best practice toward letting nonhuman trees, fungi, and animals lead.[^roudavskiled]

1. **Retain coarse woody debris, fallen logs, and leaf litter where they fall, and favour larger and more decayed pieces.**
   - **Actions**: leave fallen branches, logs, bark, and litter in situ; halt clearing, chipping, and tidying; favour large-diameter, advanced-decay pieces and a mix of sizes. This supports the Tree capability to Communicate and the model's Decay proposal.
   - **Evidence**: large trees are disproportionate suppliers of debris and litter that younger trees cannot provide, and coarse woody debris stores nutrients and organic carbon, traps mobilised soil particles and organic litter, provides microsites for seedling establishment, and supports stronger biodiversity and soil-function responses when pieces are larger, older, and more decayed.[^leroux2014][^frohlich2020][^killey2010][^mallencooper2026]

2. **Let dead wood accumulate passively in retained patches.**
   - **Actions**: define patches where managers add no debris but remove none either, and let fallen and cut trees form dead wood on site over years. This supports the Decay proposal and the Buffer intervention.
   - **Evidence**: in Helsinki's urban forests, dead-wood volumes track how long a patch has been left alone, from a median of 10.1 cubic metres per hectare in random urban forest to 115.6 in semi-natural forest. In Kraków, coarse woody debris declines as property prices rise, because wealthier districts tidy fallen and dead wood away, so its absence in groomed areas is a management signal,
   - Further details:
     - In woodland, scattered trees concentrate nutrients and litter beneath their canopies and shelter the seedbed, doubling as nurse sites for the next cohort (Prober & Thiele 2005; Manning, Fischer & Lindenmayer 2006).
     - Coarse woody debris holds a large reserve of nutrients and organic carbon and releases it slowly as it decays, so it sustains site productivity and soil organic carbon rather than letting nutrients leach away (Killey, McElhinny, Rayner & Wood 2010).
     - Decaying wood intercepts mobilised soil particles and organic litter, reducing erosion and the loss of resources from a site (Killey et al. 2010)
     - Soil beside coarse woody debris in degraded eucalypt woodland is significantly higher in carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and nitrate, so a fallen log builds a fertile patch around itself (Goldin & Hutchinson 2013); in semi-arid mulga, contour-stacked branch piles trapped soil, water, and litter and raised soil nitrogen, carbon, infiltration, respiration, and fauna from bare ground (Tongway & Ludwig 1996)
     - Woody debris also buffers temperature and moisture extremes and captures seed, generating distinct plant communities around it, and acts as a nursery for litter accumulation and fungal growth a cleared stand loses for decades (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026; Manning, Cunningham & Lindenmayer 2013).
     - Decay releases staggered pulses: nitrogen availability rises as lignin breaks down and nitrogen-fixing bacteria colonise the wood, and calcium rises, while potassium leaches early, so a log feeds the soil different nutrients at different stages (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026; Laiho & Prescott 2004).
     - Larger and older pieces do more: diversity rose ~15 per cent and abundance ~15 per cent per extra 10 cm of debris diameter and abundance ~14 per cent per decade on the ground, because large pieces hold distinct bark, sapwood, and heartwood substrates and pass through a long decomposer succession (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026).
     - Large senescing trees supply most of the wood: a 100 cm diameter tree is ~10 times more likely to produce fallen debris than a 50 cm tree and produces ~10 times the volume, a Yellow Box can take over 200 years to reach that size, and one fallen bole 1 m across and 10 m long holds ~10 m3 of coarse woody debris (Killey et al. 2010).
     - Raking away a tree's own leaf litter cut soil decomposition 17 per cent and soil carbon up to 24 per cent, a legacy effect that re-retaining leaves did not reverse in 1-2 years (Ferlauto, Schmitt & Burghardt 2024); a large eucalypt drops ~10 times more litter under its crown than adjacent grass (12.5 vs 1.27 t/ha), building a fertile nutrient island around its own trunk (McElhinny et al. 2009).ot a baseline.[^korhonen2020][^frohlich2020]

3. **Let trees age, senesce, die, and decompose in place, and manage human risk with understorey and buffer zones instead of removal.**
   - **Actions**: permit trees to progress through ageing, snag, fallen, and decomposed stages on site; plant dense understorey and define drop zones beneath ageing crowns; reserve removal for hazards no spatial measure can manage; where removal of non-native stands is unavoidable, stage it slowly in patches over five to ten years and leave standing dead trees as transitional habitat. This supports the Decay proposal and the Buffer intervention.
   - **Evidence**: useful-life metrics can treat trees as amenities, whereas decay and collapse produce the hollows, dead wood, and litter many lifeforms rely on. Ginninderry shows mature-tree retention at the peri-urban fringe: retained remnant-tree proportions were far higher than a cited Canberra average, and restoration treatments under old hollow-bearing red gum and yellow box trees used native tussock boundaries, reduced mowing, timber, mulch, native grasses, forbs, acacias, and fallen timber retention.[^roudavski2021][^epsdd2023]

4. **Reduce or eliminate canopy pruning so crowns can spread.**
   - **Actions**: scale routine pruning to a minimum, and remove canopy pruning entirely where clearances allow, so trees develop large limbs, peeling bark, and dead branches. This supports the Tree capability to Acquire Resources and the Release Control proposal.
   - **Evidence**: large trees provide structural elements such as large limbs, peeling bark, and dead branches that younger or repeatedly pruned trees do not offer. Intensive pruning around infrastructure removes large branches, keeps trees small, and simplifies their structure; felling or heavily pruning trees before they reach full biological potential reduces their value to wildlife.[^leroux2014][^grossmann2020][^stagoll2012]

5. **Retain and reuse non-native trees and prosthetic habitat.**
   - **Actions**: keep introduced trees as roosts, perches, bark substrates, and epiphyte substrates rather than removing them by default; pair retained trees with artificial hollows, bark sleeves, installed mistletoe, and standing dead non-native stems where appropriate. This supports the Deploy Structure proposal and the Host service.
   - **Evidence**: Powerful Owls use non-native trees as roosts, so removing them can remove regular roost habitat. Non-native trees can carry epiphytes, lichens, and invertebrate-rich bark; erected dead trees and utility poles enriched with hollows and perches can raise native bird richness where mature trees have been cleared, though these structures support fewer species than living mature trees. Mistletoe reintroduction also shows how existing urban trees can become host structures.[^bradsworth2021][^grossmann2020][^hannan2019][^watson2023]

6. **Protect soil, mycorrhizal networks, and root space from compaction and severance.**
   - **Actions**: keep soil under and around trees uncompacted and unsealed; avoid trenching and root severance; retain litter and decomposing wood that feed soil biota. This protects the Tree capability to Communicate.
   - **Evidence**: city trees depend on mycorrhizal interactions that increase soil porosity, water retention, and structure, yet urban habitats show reduced mycorrhizal colonisation.[^stevenson2020] Roudavski and Davis identify compacted, impermeable surfaces and insufficient root space as conditions that confine urban trees.[^roudavski2021] Rebuilt soil shows the size of the loss, since de-compacted, deep-composted ground grew up to 84 per cent more canopy over six years at constrained sites.[^layman2016]

7. **Reallocate road and parking space beneath ageing trees into collapse and habitat zones.**
   - **Actions**: convert parking bays, lane sections, and other sealed surfaces beneath ageing crowns into depaved habitat islands where trees can fall and decompose, and link these islands as nearby trees collapse. This gives the Buffer intervention the space it needs.
   - permit trees to progress through ageing, snag, fallen, and decomposed stages on site; plant dense understorey and define drop zones beneath ageing crowns; reserve removal for hazards no spatial measure can manage; where removal of non-native stands is unavoidable, stage it slowly in patches over five to ten years and leave standing dead trees as transitional habitat. This supports the Decay proposal and the Buffer intervention.

   - **Evidence**: Roudavski and Davis propose that street planting expand understorey and reallocate space as the spatial influence of cars decreases.
   - Redundant car parking: Modelling in Melbourne shows that streets are 26% of central Melbourne land, on-street parking 21% of that; up to half could fit existing garages within 200 m, freeing ~50 ha, growing 31-59 ha of canopy and de-paving 6.6-24.5 ha, ~a third of the 40%-by-2040 target (Croeser et al. 2022).
   - The Ginninderry development on the peri-urban fringe  as an example of retaining mature trees, showing the increasing interest in developments at the peri urban fringe [^epsdd2023].  Ginninderry retained far more remnant trees than typical ACT greenfield development: 78%, 92%, and 86% retention across stages, compared with a cited Canberra average of 37.3%.
     > Ginninderry also trialled treatments under remnant trees: traditional mowing, mulch/mass planting, and ecological restoration. The latter two leave fallen branches, introduce logs, and plant Eucalyptus seedlings as future cohorts. Fowles Street Park restored five 200-300-year-old hollow-bearing red gum/yellow box trees using native tussock boundaries, reduced mowing, timber, mulch, native grasses/forbs/acacias, and fallen timber retention.

8. **Sustain multi-aged, structurally diverse cohorts rather than even-aged replacement plantings.**
   - **Actions**: plant and retain trees across a spread of ages, species, and genera; keep senescent stems standing alongside young recruits; avoid removing and replacing whole even-aged avenues at once. This sustains Tree capabilities across generations.
   - **Evidence**: scattered trees are keystone structures whose loss can trigger regime shifts, so landscapes must balance recruitment and mortality across ages. Large trees support distinct wildlife, including raptors and threatened parrots that occur almost exclusively at large trees. The City of Melbourne's diversity guidelines recommend no more than 5 per cent of any species, 10 per cent of any genus, and 20 per cent of any family by 2040, reducing the chance that a single pest or pathogen removes a large share of canopy at once.[^manning2006][^leroux2018][^melbourne2011diversity][^stevenson2020]

## Experimental ways to improve tree habitat in modified ecosystems and cities
The next four supports are promising but thinly evidenced

1. **Engineer ageing trees to stay standing and habitat-bearing.**
   - **Actions**: beyond allowing decay, use the veteran-tree toolkit: phased retrenchment pruning to mimic natural crown dieback, coronet cuts that leave fractured ends rather than flat saw faces, propping and dynamic slack cable-bracing that preserve movement, and monolithing a tree otherwise felled into a stabilised standing trunk. On introduced clones such as the elm, bring hollows forward by sub-lethal veteranisation, ring-barking, or pollarding. This supports the Buffer intervention and the Deploy Structure proposal.
   - **Evidence**: phased retrenchment and coronet cutting keep top-heavy veterans from collapse while retaining features of age, and pollarding accelerates hollow formation; erected dead trees and hollow-enriched poles raise bird richness where mature trees were cleared, though they carry fewer species than living old trees. No Melbourne or eucalypt-specific trials of these techniques were found.[^fay2002][^sebek2013][^hannan2019]

2. **Build Common Mycorrhizal Networks (CMNs).**
   Common Mycorrhizal Networks (CMNs) are shared fungal mycelial networks that can connect the roots of compatible plants and create pathways for water, nutrients, carbon, and chemical signals to move through soil. In built environments this remains an exploratory design aim rather than a settled intervention: Harden and Moreno-Mateos describe the relevant supports as soil permeability, structured soils, cautious inoculation, soil conduits, and planting schemes that align mycorrhizal types.[^harden2026]
   Evidence for CMNs is mixed: Harden and Moreno-Mateos note that their relevance has been questioned, while other studies report carbon transfer and positive effects on plant growth, survival, and community structure, with urban applications still underexplored.[^harden2026]

   - Permeable surfaces: help water/oxygen, but block organic litter reaching soil — a trade-off for decomposer fungi.
   - Structured soils: stone-matrix/sandy-loam mixes that bear load while allowing root growth.
   - Mycorrhizal inoculation: this is the most caveated section. Inoculation can aid drought tolerance and disease resistance, but: success depends on species pairing and the existing indigenous inoculum potential; fertilizers may act antagonistically (Yuan 2025); a meta-analysis found commercial inoculants ineffective vs. soil from a rural forest (Maltz & Treseder 2015 — your [^sommerville2020]/inoculant point); and inoculation can backfire by introducing invasive AM isolates or pathogens, or outcompeting resident fungi (Schwartz 2006, Antunes 2009).
   - Increasing soil connectivity — soil conduits: open-air trenches (≥15 cm wide, ~30 cm soil depth + crushed-stone drainage, mulch top, metal grate) connecting street trees to each other and to parks/groves. Modeled on wildlife overpasses and pollinator corridors. Explicitly a prototype: "remains at a prototype stage and requires systematic testing." Open questions they list: how many conduits for functional connectivity, optimal length/diameter, same or different mycorrhizal types. Suggested first test: whether connected soils have higher inoculum potential than unconnected.
   - Build unified networks of multiple fungi type connected through ‘bridging plants’ that associate with both types of fungus). Planting schemes: build CMNs by grouping same-mycorrhizal-type plants (e.g. AM overstory Acer/Pyrus + AM shrubs Rubus/Digitalis); use "dual-mycorrhizal bridge" species (Acacia, Alnus, Eucalyptus, Fraxinus, Populus, Salix, Shorea, Uapaca; Teste 2019) to link AM and ECM patches into one network. Rests on Beiler et al. 2009 (the Douglas-fir "wood-wide web" Rhizopogon study).

3. **Enable natural recruitment and rewild larger ground patches.**
   - **Actions**: open moist, low-nutrient, weed-free seedbeds beneath and downwind of seed trees, restore the flood or disturbance cue, cut mowing and trampling, and protect the seedlings that appear. This supports the Tree capability to Reproduce and the Recruit proposal.
   - **Evidence**: scattered trees act as recruitment nuclei and fertility islands, so the challenge is to balance recruitment and mortality in the right spatial pattern.[^manning2006]
   - eucalypts self-seed within the drip-line and River Red Gum keys recruitment to receding floods, yet Canberra greenspace held 25 seedlings per hectare against 315 in reserves, a thirteenfold deficit that is a management artefact, not an inability. Berlin contains 337 hectares of forest nobody planted, with no shortage of native tree regeneration, and Blois shows how bare, permeable ground can recruit species once herbicide pressure stops.[^leroux2014][^distefano2002][^kowarik2019][^bonthoux2019]

4. **Explore Miyawaki and micro-forests.**
   - **Actions**: use dense multi-layered native plantings for soil preparation, learning, and small patches, and prefer applied nucleation, planted islands that let birds and bats import the rest, where the aim is self-extending woodland. This supports the Recruit proposal at small scale.
   - **Evidence**: a systematic review found the Miyawaki method's rapid-growth, succession, self-sustainability, biodiversity, and carbon claims weak to null and its maturity claim unevidenced, whereas applied nucleation matched full plantation recovery at a third of the cost over fifteen years; neither substitutes for the century-scale processes of old canopy, hollows, deadwood, and animal-dispersed fungi.[^morales2026][^holl2020]

## Melbourne Applicability

The strongest evidence transfer to Melbourne comes from temperate-Australian studies of large trees, hollows, and coarse woody debris, and from Melbourne's own strategies, which already treat the urban forest as habitat. *Living Melbourne* defines that forest in the broadest sense, as all the trees, shrubs, grasses, soil, and water on public and private land, and notes that large trees are disproportionate providers of the hollows and coarse woody debris many fauna need.[^livingmelbourne2019] Metropolitan canopy is only about 15 per cent and ranges from 4 per cent in the west to 25 per cent in the east, residential land holds 58 per cent of it, and half the city runs 5°C above its non-urban baseline.[^livingmelbourne2019] Lorimer records that clearing reduced the region's native vegetation by the turn of the twentieth century, so today's forests are overwhelmingly young, dense regrowth, and the large old trees that supply hollows are scarce by history, not only by management.[^lorimer2011]

- Metropolitan Melbourne canopy is just 15%, from 25% (east) to 4% (west); half the city runs 5C above its non-urban baseline, hot spots under 3% canopy with no tall trees (Living Melbourne 2019).
- City of Melbourne core: 11% canopy across public and private (89% without natural shade); almost 43% of trees are one family (Myrtaceae); plane trees alone are 75% of the central-city forest (City of Melbourne 2012).
- Retention is decisive: mature-removal rate vs canopy gain r < -0.83; ambitious targets need ~1%/yr mature removal, slip out of reach above 3%; real rates run 2.28-7% (Croeser et al. 2025). Large trees give ~75% more environmental benefit than small ones (City of Melbourne 2012).

Urban trees usually live under combined stress:

- sealed surfaces that block rainfall infiltration and gas exchange;
- compacted soils and small rootable volumes;
- heat, drought, water restrictions, and warmer futures;
- pollution, salts, heavy metals, and traffic stress;
- trenching, utilities, root severance, construction access and vehicle damage;
- overhead-wire and tram-clearance pruning;
- vandalism and young-tree establishment failure;
- risk assessment, public fear, liability, and useful-life accounting.

### Applicable in Melbourne

1. **Retain deadwood and litter**: keep coarse woody debris, fallen logs, leaf litter, and standing dead stems in parks, boulevards, and reserves, and favour larger and more decayed pieces.
2. **Let ageing trees complete more of their life cycle**: allow trees to senesce, die, and decompose in place, and manage human risk through understorey planting and drop zones rather than default removal.
3. **Reduce canopy pruning where possible**: where clearances allow, let crowns spread and develop hollows, dead branches, and peeling bark.
4. **Retain non-native habitat trees**: keep non-native trees as owl roosts, epiphyte substrates, and bark habitat, and stage any removal slowly in patches.
5. **Protect root zones and soil continuity**: protect soil and root zones from compaction, severance, and sealing, and retain the litter and decomposing wood that sustain mycorrhizal networks.
6. **Sustain multi-aged cohorts**: keep multi-aged, multi-species cohorts under the existing diversity targets, with senescent stems alongside young recruits.

These actions match the ecology of Melbourne's large trees, including River Red Gum and other eucalypts whose hollows take well over a century to form, and the introduced English elm that dominates the inner city's ageing canopy. They also match stated policy, since *Living Melbourne* and the Urban Forest Strategy 2012–2032 commit Melbourne to a connected, habitat-bearing forest and to roughly doubling municipal canopy by 2040.[^livingmelbourne2019][^melbourne2012strategy] Retention is the binding constraint, because mature-tree removal correlates strongly and negatively with canopy gain, ambitious targets need removal held near 1 per cent a year, and real rates run 2.28 to 7 per cent.[^croeser2025] Biodiversity-sensitive urban design supplies the framework that turns canopy targets into onsite habitat through its five principles of maintaining and introducing habitat, facilitating dispersal, minimising threats, facilitating natural ecological processes, and improving human-nature interactions.[^garrard2018]

### Transferrable with local calibration

1. **Artificial hollows and veteranisation**: these transfer to Melbourne, but managers should calibrate cavity dimensions, wound placement, and materials to local hollow-using fauna and to eucalypt and elm wood, and treat prosthetic dead-tree or habitat-pole structures as a complement to retained living trees, not a replacement.[^hannan2019][^ibarra2020]
2. **Recruitment and rewilding patches**: these transfer, but practitioners should match seedling density, species mix, and soil preparation to Melbourne's drier climate, flashy runoff, and impervious surfaces.[^leroux2014]
3. **Passive deadwood accumulation**: this transfers, but volumes will build slowly from a low base and must overcome the same property-driven tidying that suppresses deadwood elsewhere.[^korhonen2020][^frohlich2020]
4. **Mature-tree retention at growth fronts**: the Ginninderry model transfers to Melbourne's growth fronts, but the inner city must pair retention with depaving and prosthetic habitat rather than open setbacks.[^epsdd2023]
5. **Road and parking reallocation**: this transfers, but its scale and timing should track local kerbside demand and heritage constraints, building on evidence that up to half of Melbourne's on-street parking could move into nearby garages and free 31 to 59 hectares of canopy.[^roudavski2021][^croeser2022]
** fungal connections and eucalyptus ** post-fire, Tasmanian bettong digging for underground truffles jumped up to tenfold within a month, pulse-dispersing the ectomycorrhizal fungi eucalypts regenerate with, a tight animal-fungus-fire-tree loop almost entirely missing from city soils (Johnson 1995). [to do: check to see melbourne contexts]

### Melbourne-Focused Implementation Priorities

1. **Parade (an ageing-elm boulevard)**: retain the senescent elms through their transition into snags and fallen wood rather than replacing whole even-aged sections; convert parking bays and lane edges beneath the crowns into depaved drop zones planted with understorey, so trees collapse safely and link into connected grassland that supports recruitment of a mixed-age successor canopy.
2. **Street (young native street trees)**: reduce risk-averse pruning and debris clearing so young eucalypts develop habitat structure; fit artificial hollows and erect habitat poles to bridge the century-long gap before natural cavities form; convert parking beneath trees into buffer zones where crowns grow unpruned and nurse logs accumulate.
3. **City (infrastructure-dominated surfaces)**: protect and depave root zones to relieve compaction; translocate fallen stems onto load-bearing surfaces as elevated habitat; reallocate fragments of roof, facade, and ground into continuous habitat through bio-envelopes.
4. **Procurement and maintenance**: write the retention of senescent stems, coarse woody debris, and drop zones into routine maintenance specifications, and procure long-term habitat services that fund biological, hybrid, and artificial structures over decades rather than one-off installations.
5. **Useful-life assessment and governance**: revise useful-life assessment so decay, hollow formation, and collapse count as contributions rather than failures, and reconcile the plan to remove around 55 per cent of elms within a decade and retain only about 4 per cent of eucalypts beyond 60 years with the timescales over which hollows and dead wood develop.[^melbourne2012strategy][^leroux2014] Mature removal must stay near 1 per cent a year for any canopy target to hold.[^croeser2025]

## Featured species 1: English Elm (*Ulmus procera*)

The most prominent large tree along Melbourne's heritage boulevards and the being that anchors the 'Parade' place. About 400 trees, mostly English elm with a small admixture of Dutch elm (*Ulmus* x *hollandica*), stand in four rows along Royal Parade in Parkville, planted in 1913 and protected on the Victorian Heritage Register since 2009.[^nationaltrustelm][^melbourne2015parkville]. These are the largest English-elm stand on Earth, alive only because the disease that erased it elsewhere never crossed quarantine (Yau 1982; Croeser et al. 2020). They live as a managed cohort of near-identical clones: people graft, plant, water, prune, and assess them, and the same heritage status that keeps the avenue standing frames each tree as an amenity whose decline triggers removal.

**Size**: 25 to 35 m tall at maturity, with a broad arching crown spreading 15 to 20 m and a single massive bole over a metre in diameter. A large old elm carries an order of magnitude more bark, branch, and canopy surface than a young replacement, and an inner-Melbourne specimen of this size approaches 1,000 kg of standing biomass.[^disney2018]

**Origin**: Molecular work identifies English elm as a single, ancient clone linked to Roman propagation, probably transported as root suckers, with efficient vegetative reproduction and rare seed set. In direct terms, the English elm persists by cloning itself sideways through suckers rather than by reliable seed production.[^gil2004] The closest ecological comparator is therefore small-leaved European field elm lineages, often associated with fertile, moist, riparian, floodplain, edge and human-managed landscapes rather than a single untouched woodland habitat.[^armstrong1996][^elm-notes]

**Mobility**: Elms throw up root suckers that creep outward from the parent and can colonise unmanaged soil as clonal thickets. Across Victoria, English elm is naturalised largely through suckering from nearby parent trees rather than from seed; in managed urban settings this can be treated as a maintenance or weed risk as well as a persistence strategy.[^vicfloraulmus]

**Evolved conditions**: Wild European elms are trees of cool, moist, mixed broadleaved forest on fertile soils, clustering along rivers, streams, and floodplains, and *U. minor*, the lineage closest to *U. procera*, is the most riparian and edge-associated of them.[^caudullo2016] A cool-climate floodplain tree now stands on hot, dry, sealed urban ground.

**Adaptability**: It is a tree that can tolerate pruning and damage up to a point because dormant and adventitious buds can produce shoots; Thomas specifically notes exuberant basal shoots in English elm.[^thomas2014] Melbourne's heavy clay loam and impervious clay-pan can suit shallow-rooted elms better than deeper-rooted species in some street situations, but sealed surfaces, high water tables, trenching, gas leaks and heat still make the street an unstable root habitat.[^yau1982]

It is far less able to meet a hotter, drier climate, and Melbourne's tree-vulnerability assessment places *U. procera* and *U.* x *hollandica* in its highest future-temperature risk category.[^kendal2016][^vicgov2024].

- **Projected removals and vulnerability**: around 55 per cent of City of Melbourne elms are projected for removal within a decade, with diversity caps of 5 per cent species, 10 per cent genus, and 20 per cent family by 2040 deliberately retreating from exotic monocultures. Climate is expected to become the most severe threat to native species within a decade.[^melbourne2011diversity][^lorimer2011]

As a single genetic clone it is also acutely exposed to pests and disease, from elm leaf beetle to the elm bark beetle that vectors Dutch elm disease, the epidemic that erased elm avenues across the Northern Hemisphere but has not reached Australia.[^gil2004]

**Lifespan**: the elm's biological ceiling and its Melbourne working life are very different numbers, and the gap between them is the room design has to work in. In cool European woodland the closest wild comparator, the *U. minor* lineage, reaches about 300 to 400 years.[^sabatini2021] In Melbourne, well-maintained urban elms are benchmarked at roughly 100 to 150 years, and Arthur's Elms at the Royal Botanic Gardens, the oldest in Australia, are about 170.[^johnpatrick2022][^heritagevictoria2023][^edwards2012] Under ordinary boulevard care the cohort's useful life is shorter still, about 105 to 125 years against a 1913 planting, but that is the threshold at which an amenity-and-risk assessment calls for removal, not the age at which the tree would die.[^treelogic2022][^melbourne2015parkville] An elm that is irrigated, pest-managed, and left standing rather than removed when hazardous could persist well beyond that, to roughly 180 to 240 years; it would not reach the full European ceiling, because Melbourne's heat and drought, and an added risk of sudden heat-stress collapse, pull the span back toward 165 to 220 years under future climate.[^leroux2014][^kendal2016][^vicgov2024]

| State | Age (years) | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| European biological ceiling | 300–400 | Forest maxima for the *U. minor* lineage and *U. glabra* under optimum European conditions.[^sabatini2021] |
| Melbourne documented maximum | 150–200 (Arthur's Elms ~170) | Australian benchmarks for well-maintained elms, anchored to Arthur's Elms.[^johnpatrick2022][^heritagevictoria2023][^edwards2012] |
| Useful life expectancy | 105–125 | Removal threshold under boulevard care for the 1913 Royal Parade cohort, not a death age.[^treelogic2022][^melbourne2015parkville] |
| Age-in-place | 180–240 | Documented maximum plus a recovered fraction of the European gap, with trees left standing.[^leroux2014] |
| Climate-adjusted age-in-place | 165–220 | Age-in-place reduced per Melbourne's tree-vulnerability study and the 2024 climate projections.[^kendal2016][^vicgov2024] |

**Life cycle**: the elm grows fast when young, then slows and ages into a senescing crown that hollows and sheds limbs gradually. As it ages it develops the structures other beings need, deadwood in the upper canopy, shedding and furrowed bark, broken and hollowing limbs, basal cavities, and a steady fall of branches and leaves, features that take decades to a century to form and that young replacement trees do not supply.[^leroux2014]

**Habitat provided**: Melbourne's ageing elms are real habitat. At University Square 47 of 53 elms bore hollows, 255 in all, many large enough for Common Brushtail Possums, found mostly in and below the elms.[^melbourneunisquares] Powerful Owls also roost in non-native trees and their bark carries epiphytes, so removing non-indigenous trees deprives owls of regular roosts and argues for slowing the pace of removal.[^bradsworth2021]

**Communication**: like other large trees the elm signals and shares through root exudates and mycorrhizal fungi, but as an arbuscular-mycorrhizal tree it draws on a different fungal guild from the ectomycorrhizal eucalypts and cannot plug into their networks, and Melbourne's compacted, sealed boulevard soil reduces that colonisation while the avenue's isolation limits how far it connects at all.[^stevenson2020][^teste2020][^bainard2011]

**Reproduction**: the elm reproduces in two ways, and only one of them works in Melbourne. It produces pollen normally, but as a single roughly 2,000-year-old Roman clone it rarely sets viable seed, so sexual reproduction effectively fails.[^gil2004] It reproduces vigorously by vegetative root suckers instead, which is why it naturalises across Victoria, most populations forming by suckering from parent trees rather than from seed.[^vicfloraulmus] In the managed avenue, people suppress those suckers and raise replacements by grafting and planting, so genetic renewal and avenue recruitment depend on humans even though the tree itself is far from unable to reproduce.[^gil2004][^vicfloraulmus]

**Design Implications**:
*Useful-life assessment and governance*: revise useful-life assessment so decay, hollow formation, and collapse count as contributions rather than failures, and reconcile the plan to remove around 55 per cent of elms within a decade and retain only about 4 per cent of eucalypts beyond 60 years with the timescales over which hollows and dead wood develop.[^melbourne2012strategy][^leroux2014] Mature removal must stay near 1 per cent a year for any canopy target to hold.[^croeser2025]

*Already tried or planned.*

- A Powerful Owl roosts in and forages from non-native trees, so removing elms strips habitat it actively uses.[^bradsworth2021] An ageing elm also offers a substrate for epiphytes and lichens, so retaining elms rather than felling them on schedule is a near-term habitat decision, not only a heritage one.[^grossmann2020]
- Intensive pruning to keep limbs clear of wires removes the wounded, decaying, deadwood-bearing parts of the crown, so a pruning-release that frees the canopy lets the elm both grow and supply habitat.[^grossmann2020]
- An elm left to age is one of few near-term sources of slowly forming hollows, because Australian trees carry no excavating animal such as a woodpecker and form cavities only through decades of limb-death and decay.[^penton2021] Birds, reptiles, and declining mammals share these same cavities, which grow more abundant as a tree enlarges, so a large decaying elm is a keystone resource while the planted native cohort is still a century from bearing hollows.[^penton2021][^ibarra2020]
- The avenue's renewal is a human act, because the clone sets no viable seed and its only self-recruitment is the suckering that management suppresses, so the model's reproduction indicator for this being is met by human propagation rather than seedfall.[^gil2004][^vicfloraulmus]

*Speculative or more ambitious.*

- Removing a whole even-aged cohort opens a gap in habitat structure that lasts as long as those structures take to reform, a century or more, so the simultaneous removal of the Parade elms is the loss of an entire habitat stratum at once for the Bird and Lizard personas.[^melbourne2012strategy][^leroux2014]
- Fitting artificial hollows, bracing senescing limbs to fail safely, and applying sub-lethal veteranisation such as ring-barking can bring forward, on existing elms, the cavities and deadwood that decay would otherwise take decades to produce.[^hannan2019][^leroux2014] Because the elm is an introduced clone rather than a remnant native, intervening on the wood itself is defensible here.
- Native mistletoe can be added to the elm as living canopy habitat. A City of Melbourne trial established native creeping mistletoe (*Muellerina eucalyptoides*) on London plane trees, and *Ulmus* is among its known exotic hosts, so a healthy long-retention elm is a credible host scaffold for a monitored trial that adds nectar, fruit, dense roosting foliage, and enriched litter to an introduced crown.[^watson2023]
- The elm's suckering weediness is the same vigour that keeps this disease-free clone alive as one of the world's most significant mature elm populations, since Dutch elm disease bypassed Australia.[^gil2004][^vicfloraulmus] Managing sucker spread at sensitive boundaries while recruiting a mixed-age, mixed-species successor canopy keeps the heritage being and its habitat without licensing escape or denying decline.[^kendal2016][^vicgov2024]

## Featured species 2: River Red Gum (*Eucalyptus camaldulensis*)

The largest and longest-lived native tree of Melbourne's watercourses and floodplains, the defining canopy tree of the River Red Gum Woodland that lined the Birrarung (Yarra) and the volcanic-plains creeks before colonisation, and the most widely distributed eucalypt on the continent.[^wikicamaldulensis][^moore2019] It is the representative tree in this paper's model, so featuring it keeps the evidence base consistent with the 180-year maturation horizon the simulation adopts.[^rutten2024][^leroux2014] Where the elm depends on people, the River Red Gum depends on water.

**Size**: typically 20 m tall but reaching 45 m, with a broad spreading crown and a trunk that thickens for centuries.[^wikicamaldulensis][^leroux2014] Bark is smooth and white, cream, or grey, shedding in slabs and ribbons to expose patches of yellow, pink, and brown, with rough flaky bark persisting near the base.[^wikicamaldulensis]

**Mobility**: the tree stays where it germinates, but unlike the human-planted elm it disperses itself by water. Its buoyant seed rafts on receding floodwaters, floats for about 36 hours, and travels kilometres downstream to seed even-aged strips along the flood line.[^wikicamaldulensis][^distefano2002]

**Evolved conditions**: the River Red Gum expects water process. It belongs to floodplains, creek lines, billabong margins, and wetland soils, stood co-dominant with Yellow Box across Melbourne's precolonial grassy woodlands, and keys its whole life to flooding, recession, and groundwater.[^wikicamaldulensis][^presland2005] It tolerates immersion for many months and recruits only when floods recede and leave bare moist soil, the opposite of the elm's dry, sealed boulevard.[^distefano2002]

**Adaptability**: the tree survives scars, drought, fire, and limb loss, resprouting from epicormic buds and a lignotuber, so its plasticity is biological rather than the elm's reliance on human care.[^moore2019] Its vulnerability is hydrological, not bureaucratic, because where river regulation removes the flood pulse, adult condition and recruitment both decline and stands become non-recruiting relics.[^distefano2002]

**Lifespan**: it lives 400 to 1,000 years, so the trees Melbourne calls ancient began before the city, and it carries habitat far longer than the elm's 100 to 240 year urban span.[^moore2019] It grows fast, so it bears fewer hollows per unit of diameter than the boxes, yet reaches such size that it dominates riverine hollows, which begin to form only after about 120 to 180 years.[^moore2019][^leroux2014]

**Life cycle**: it grows fast when young then slowly thickens for centuries, ageing into broad limbs, scars, dead branches, loose and rough bark, and hollows, and stands as a dead tree for decades afterward.[^wikicamaldulensis][^lindenmayer2017small] Hollow abundance rises steeply with diameter: across the northern Victorian plains fewer than 1 per cent of trees 10 to 30 cm across bore hollows, 13 per cent of trees 30 to 70 cm did, and 68 per cent of trees over 70 cm did, so only a large old tree fully supplies cavities for the Bird and Lizard personas.[^bennett1994]

**Communication**: the River Red Gum signals and shares above and below ground. Summer flowers carry so much nectar and pollen that a tree in flower hums with bees, feeding insects, birds, and small mammals.[^wikicamaldulensis] Below ground it partners ectomycorrhizal fungi, many of them hypogeous truffles that fruit underground and cannot travel on the wind, so they depend on digging mammals such as potoroos and bettongs to eat and spread their spores, a fungus, mammal, and fire loop largely missing from the city.[^maser2008][^johnson1995]

**Reproduction**: the River Red Gum recruits itself, but only on water's terms. Seed stored in woody capsules falls to bare wet ground as floods recede, germinates in pulses, and survives where seedlings reach subsoil water before summer, an episodic event that historically occurred only a handful of times a century.[^distefano2002] Sealed and channelised urban surfaces suppress this, so reproduction at the stand scale depends on opening soil and restoring inundation rather than on planting, the reverse of the elm's human-propagated renewal.[^distefano2002][^leroux2014]

**Design Implications**:

- Large eucalypts act as keystone structures in urban parks, with bird richness, abundance, and breeding all rising with diameter, and adding trees over 100 cm raised woodland-bird richness by about 300 per cent in Canberra parks, so no young replacement on sealed ground substitutes for a large old River Red Gum.[^stagoll2012][^leroux2014]
- Scattered large trees carry exceptional value, supporting raptors, the threatened Superb Parrot, hollow-nesters, and nectarivores that smaller trees do not, so even a single retained River Red Gum acts as a node and stepping stone for the Bird persona.[^leroux2018]
- Recruitment is the hidden bottleneck, so the design lever is hydrological: depave and open moist ground, restore seasonal inundation, and protect flood-cued seedlings from mowing and trampling rather than relying on planting alone.[^distefano2002][^leroux2014]
- Standing dead River Red Gums and fallen logs keep providing hollows, perches, bark, and ground refuge for decades after death and store large amounts of carbon, so letting these trees decompose in place is itself a design act, and a felled 200-year-old tree is an effectively irreplaceable loss.[^lindenmayer2017small][^rutten2024]

## Featured species 3: Yellow Box (*Eucalyptus melliodora*)

The honey-scented keystone of the critically endangered Box-Gum Grassy Woodland, the community that once covered the fertile plains north of Melbourne and was cleared first, so under 5 per cent remains.[^rawlings2010][^dsewpc2012] Where the River Red Gum holds the wettest ground, Yellow Box holds the fertile dry plains that farming wanted most.

**Size**: 15 to 30 m tall, with a variable crown and short, often crooked bole; persists for many hundreds of years.[^banks1997] Bark ranges from yellowish-brown and flaky on the lower trunk to smooth above.

**Preferred habitat**: fertile, well-drained loams of the inland plains and lower slopes, in grassy woodland alongside White Box and Blakely's Red Gum.[^dsewpc2012] Because these soils were the first ploughed, the tree now survives mostly as scattered paddock veterans and roadside remnants.[^deccw2011]

**Basic lifestyle**: a premier nectar tree, Yellow Box flowers irregularly, often only every second year, a feast-or-famine resource that mobile honeyeaters and lorikeets track across the landscape.[^rawlings2010][^bennett1994] It is a slower-growing box than the River Red Gum, so it forms more hollows per unit of diameter, and its slow-decaying timber holds those hollows for long periods.[^rawlings2010][^bennett1994]

**Design Implications**:

- Slow box growth means more hollows per diameter, so a Yellow Box of modest size can already carry cavities a faster-grown gum of the same girth would not, which makes retaining mid-sized paddock veterans a direct hollow-supply decision for the Bird and Lizard personas.[^bennett1994]
- Irregular feast-or-famine flowering ties nectarivores to whole networks of trees rather than single sites, so isolated Yellow Box veterans are worth retaining as stepping stones in the wider nectar landscape.[^rawlings2010]
- Box-Gum Grassy Woodland was cleared first and earliest, so the few large Yellow Box that remain are disproportionately old and irreplaceable, and recruitment on fertile, now-farmed or now-sealed plains is the limiting step for the next cohort.[^dsewpc2012][^leroux2014]

### Native large trees of the Melbourne region

| Species | Common name | Origin | Mature height and typical lifespan | Role in Melbourne and notable habitat value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *Eucalyptus camaldulensis* | River Red Gum | Native (floodplains and waterways) | 20–45 m; commonly 400–1,000 years[^lindenmayer2017small][^leroux2014] | Defining floodplain tree of the Maribyrnong, Yarra, and volcanic plains; forms abundant hollows in old age and is a keystone hollow and perch provider for birds, mammals, and reptiles[^bennett1994][^stagoll2012] |
| *Eucalyptus melliodora* | Yellow Box | Native (grassy woodland) | 15–30 m; many hundreds of years[^banks1997] | Honey-scented keystone of the critically endangered Box-Gum Grassy Woodland north of Melbourne; slow-grown trunks form more hollows per diameter, and irregular flowering feeds mobile honeyeaters[^rawlings2010][^bennett1994] |
| *Eucalyptus viminalis* | Manna Gum | Native (valleys and foothills) | 20–40 m; several centuries | Ribbon-bark riparian and foothill tree; named for the sugary manna that feeds gliders, honeyeaters, and pardalotes, and prime koala browse[^bok2025][^rutten2024] |
| *Eucalyptus ovata* | Swamp Gum (Black Gum) | Native (poorly drained flats) | 15–30 m; several centuries | Wet-ground woodland tree whose nectar and pollen feed nectarivorous birds, including the endangered Swift Parrot (*Lathamus discolor*)[^hingston2011] |
| *Eucalyptus leucoxylon* | Yellow Gum | Native (plains woodland) | 10–30 m; several centuries | One of Melbourne's most-planted eucalypt street trees; a winter nectar source that feeds honeyeaters and lorikeets in the cold season, and old stems form hollows[^stagoll2012] |
| *Corymbia maculata* | Spotted Gum | Native (south-eastern Australia, widely planted) | 25–40 m; several centuries | A *Corymbia* reaching Victoria naturally only in far East Gippsland, so in Melbourne it lives entirely as a planted, out-of-range tree; provides nectar, perches, and, when old, hollows[^stagoll2012] |
| *Allocasuarina cunninghamiana* (formerly *Casuarina*) | River She-oak | Native (riverbanks) | 15–35 m; commonly 100–200+ years | Riparian tree of the Yarra and tributaries; seed cones feed black cockatoos and the dense canopy offers roosting cover[^stagoll2012] |
| *Acacia melanoxylon* | Blackwood | Native (gullies and damp forest) | 15–30 m; commonly 100+ years | Long-lived wattle of moist gullies; flowers feed insects and birds, and old trunks develop hollows and bark habitat[^rutten2024] |
