## Examples

- Melbourne gave its trees email addresses for maintenance reports and received thousands of love letters instead, and staff began replying on a tree's behalf.[^phillips2018][^straughan2022]
- A firefighter broke a city elm's branch fighting a fire, then could not sleep and emailed an apology, writing that a building shelters only a person but a tree creates habitat for the whole world.[^straughan2022]
- Manna is real sugar a person can pick off a Manna Gum leaf, mostly raffinose and sucrose, and it feeds sugar gliders, honeyeaters, and the endangered forty-spotted pardalote.[^bok2025]
- A radio-tracked Powerful Owl spent the day in an exotic Monterey pine clutching a ringtail possum, and roosted in exotic trees on all but one occasion, so weed-tree removal must be staged.[^mcnabb2011]
- A baroque park built round a small-leaved lime (*Tilia cordata*) avenue planted in 1684 held 18 red-listed beetle species, three of them dependent on a fungus that grows only on old limes.[^jonsell2004]
- A Fairfield couple secretly fed bath and shower water to a neighbour's tree through the drought so the council would not remove it.[^pearce2015]
- When Blois stopped using herbicide, plants self-recruited to nearly full cover, 307 species across 48 km, about a fifth of the regional flora, and the binding constraint was bare soil, not seed supply.[^bonthoux2019]
- Hollows are made of time, not beaks: with no excavating animal in Australia, a eucalypt forms its first cavities only after 120 to 220 years of limb-death and decay.[^gibbons2002][^lindenmayer1993]

## Further Details on Specific Interventions and Processes

In no particular order...

### Age-in-place engineering toolkit: keeping ageing or declining trees standing safely.

- **Cabling and bracing, dynamic vs static**: static systems fix a defect under tension; dynamic systems install with slack, act preventively, and preserve branch movement. Static cabling "can disturb or stop the natural aging process... which often includes a natural retrenchment process and branch breakage" (VetCert 2019). Cabling is explicitly a retention tool used instead of heavy pruning that would expose non-durable heartwood. Evidence status: established.
- **Dead-end stop terminations**: Smiley's dead-end stop method threads the cable through a cable-width hole, removing two weak points; double-swage stops failed near the cable's own breaking strength (7.6 kN), but the flexible dead-end abraded its hole open in 39 per cent of cases over five years. Cobra dynamic synthetic-rope bracing is non-invasive and has an approximately 12-year life, but product efficacy data are thin. Evidence status: emerging.[^smiley2011]
- **Propping / exoskeletons**: rigid ground-anchored props support over-leveraged limbs/leaning trunks; iconic cases the Angel Oak and the 11th-century Crouch Oak (three bespoke props). Practitioner evidence (ATF/Lonsdale 2013).
- **Retrenchment pruning**: Fay's method mimics natural peripheral dieback, phased over 12 to 30 years in 3 to 5 year cycles, with a first stage of 10 to 20 per cent, to stop a top-heavy veteran collapsing while retaining habitat features associated with ageing. Evidence status: established in veteran-tree practice.[^fay2002]
- **Coronet cuts** ("natural fracture pruning"): shape a cut to resemble a storm-shattered end, seeding fungal/invertebrate microhabitat instead of an "unnatural flat plane-surface... not found in nature" (Fay 2003).
- **Monolithing**: retain a tree that would normally be felled as a reduced, stabilised standing trunk (usually 4-6 m) of deadwood habitat; founding case Ashtead Common (after a fire killed ~10% of 2,000+ veteran oaks, hundreds kept as coronet-cut hulks, "well received by the public") (Alexander, Green & Key 1993; Fay 2003). Extending dead-wood techniques to living trees = **veteranisation**; pollarding accelerates hollow formation (Sebek et al. 2013).
- **Risk-managed retention** (QTRA, TRAQ, VALID): reframe "safe/unsafe" to tolerable risk (QTRA thresholds 1/1,000,000 broadly acceptable, 1/10,000 tolerable), giving managers permission to keep high-value trees. BUT no method is more reproducible than another, and "the assessor has just as much influence as the method"; QTRA training itself cut removal recommendations (Klein et al. 2023; Koeser & Smiley 2017).


### Repurposing urban space for trees

- **Reallocating road/parking**: consolidating half of Melbourne's 23,500 on-street bays into nearby garages could depave 6.6 to 24.5 ha and grow 31 to 59 ha of canopy, roughly a third of the 40-per-cent-by-2040 target. Policy precedents include Amsterdam removing about 1,500 bays per year, Paris pledging to remove half of 140,000, and New York City greening more than 600 ha from 2010 to 2020. Evidence status: established modelling and policy precedent.[^croeser2022]
- **Suspended pavement / soil cells**: a 10-year trial of elm under concrete found supported-pavement trees significantly larger in caliper than structural soils or compacted controls, with more and deeper roots (Smiley, Urban & Fite 2019). Structural cells beat structural soil and open ground over six years in Singapore, with 27.2 cm DBH compared with 24.2 and 22.3 cm (Ow & Ghosh 2017). Evidence status: established.
- **Structural soil**: over 17 years in Brooklyn, oaks under a load-bearing sidewalk matched open-tree-lawn oaks with higher survival, with roots colonising soil under pavement (Grabosky & Bassuk 2016). Evidence status: established.
- **Stockholm biochar planting beds**: the Embren method uses angular stone plus about 5 to 10 per cent biochar and compost. Stockholm adopted it after a 2001 survey found two-thirds of new trees dead or dying; mortality reportedly collapsed and six-year trees reached five times the size of 30-year trees in old pits. Evidence status: emerging practitioner reports, with biochar porosity established.
- **Permeable paving and passive irrigation**: porous pavement grew planes 29 to 51 per cent larger in stem diameter with deeper roots, while kerb-inlet raingarden tree pits both irrigate the tree and cut runoff; Melbourne has more than 200 such pits. Evidence status: established and deployed.[^mullaney2015][^croeser2022]
- **Soil volume is the master variable** (~0.6 m3 rootable soil per m2 of mature canopy; Lindsey & Bassuk): rebuilding compacted soil (subsoil + compost to 60 cm) grew 77% more trunk in one year and up to 84% more canopy over six (Layman et al. 2016); tightly kerbed pits (<10 m2) cut canopy 64-75% vs open ground (Grabosky & Gilman 2004), so enlarging openings and diverting kerbs/paths directly buys canopy and longer life.
- **Best examples**: the Melbourne redundant-parking model; the Bartlett 10-year suspended-pavement trial; the Brooklyn 17-year structural-soil street; the Stockholm city-wide retrofit.
- **Gap**: road-diet evidence is mostly mobility/stormwater, not tree growth; "room to fall and age" is absent from surface-design literature; Stockholm figures are practitioner reports.

**References**: Croeser et al. 2022 (npj Urban Sustainability 2:27); Smiley, Urban & Fite 2019 (A&UF 45:303); Ow & Ghosh 2017 (J Urban Ecology 3:jux017); Grabosky & Bassuk 2016 (UFUG 16:103); Grabosky & Gilman 2004 (J Arboriculture 30:154); Layman et al. 2016 (UFUG 16:25); Mullaney, Lucke & Trueman 2015 (LUP 134:157); Morgenroth 2011 (A&UF 37); Armson, Stringer & Ennos 2013 (UFUG 12:282); Allatt, Turner & Tarjomi 2013 (NZTA, road-space reallocation); City of Stockholm 2022 (planting-bed handbook, via TDAG).

### Autonomous recruitment + deadwood for the trees themselves

Two linked capacities: trees recruiting their own successors, and trees feeding their own soil and seedbeds through deadwood and litter. The mechanisms are the species' own designs; the human role is mostly to remove what blocks them. (The anchor citation is Killey, McElhinny, Rayner & Wood 2010, not the "Killey, Manning, Gibbons, Lindenmayer & Fischer" form.)

#### How eucalypts recruit their own successors

- Eucalypts store seed in woody capsules in the canopy and shed it within the drip-line, so recruitment concentrates beneath and downwind of the parent (Rawlings, Freudenberger & Carr 2010).
- Germination needs contact with moist, weed-free mineral soil, so a receptive seedbed (bare, burnt, disturbed, or grazed ground) is a precondition, and rank tussock or exotic sward leaves no niche (Rawlings et al. 2010).
- River Red Gum keys recruitment to receding winter and spring floodwaters and fails when floods recede too late into summer; its seed floats up to 36 hours and rafts kilometres, seeding even-aged strips along the flood line (Di Stefano 2002).
- Seedbed quality drives establishment, not just germination: Red Gum seedlings reached ~60 cm at 8-10 months on ashbed or cultivated soil versus ~10 cm on hard bare earth, because fast early growth reaches subsoil water before drought (Di Stefano 2002).
- Natural recruitment is episodic: extensive regeneration occurred only six times in Barmah forest between 1900 and 1965, set by the rare coincidence of seed, flood recession, seedbed, and summer rain, formalised as Dexter's eight interacting controls (Di Stefano 2002).
- In box-gum woodland, above-average summer rainfall is the strong germination trigger, and seed dormancy plus smoke cues let soil-stored seed wait for the right season (Rawlings et al. 2010).

#### The recruitment bottleneck, and what releases it

- Continuous grazing and superphosphate suppress regeneration across an 800,000 ha endangered ecoregion: seedling presence fell as soil nitrogen rose, and no paddock site with five or fewer trees had regenerated in 60 years (Fischer et al. 2009).
- Phosphorus enrichment shifts ground cover from native perennials to exotic annuals that then outcompete tree seedlings for the establishment-window moisture (Fischer et al. 2009; Rawlings et al. 2010).
- Releasing the bottleneck is mechanistic: fast-rotational grazing gave ~4-fold higher regeneration than continuous grazing by creating germination disturbance while sparing established seedlings (Fischer et al. 2009), and fencing raised recruits to 59 per cent of sites versus 13 per cent unfenced over 7-9 years (Spooner & Briggs 2008).
- Fencing alone is not enough where exotic annuals, elevated nutrients, and compaction remain, so reducing the autumn nitrate peak through spring burns and carbon supplements (~0.5 kg/m2 sugar or sawdust) is a direct lever back toward native seedbeds (Rawlings et al. 2010; Prober & Thiele 2005).
- In Victorian agricultural landscapes only 27 per cent of sites carried any eucalypt regeneration, contingent on a nearby seed source, soil moisture, low seed predation, and a suitable seedbed (Dorrough & Moxham 2005).

#### Self-replacing, uneven-aged stands

- Self-recruiting woodland is multi-aged (right-skewed diameter distributions, many young stems); scattered paddock trees show symmetrical distributions with no recruits, the diagnostic of a non-replacing population (Fischer et al. 2009).
- Self-replacement has hard demographic requirements: keeping scattered trees needs adult mortality below ~0.5 per cent a year, recruits exceeding existing tree numbers, and recruitment events spaced at ~15 per cent of maximum lifespan, or the landscape loses its trees within 90-180 years (Gibbons et al. 2008).
- Increasing recruitment alone cannot reverse decline if adult mortality stays high, so protecting the old trees matters as much as recruiting young ones (Gibbons et al. 2008).
- Even-aged Red Gum stands are the natural product of flood-cued recruitment, so silviculture that mimics the disturbance regime (larger gaps in frequently flooded forest, retained habitat trees) keeps the stand structurally true (Di Stefano 2002).

#### Nurse effects, facilitation, applied nucleation

- Residual and isolated trees are recruitment foci: 671 seedlings of 48 canopy species established almost entirely under residual trees, not open grass, because the crowns perch frugivorous birds and bats and import seed; the effect is structural, rising with tree height and crown area rather than fruit reward, and clumped trees recruited more species than single ones (Toh, Gillespie & Lamb 1999).
- Beneath-crown microsites also suppress competition (herbaceous biomass significantly lower under crowns) and re-establish mycorrhizal partners, so planting a few tall perch trees or clumps accelerates recovery far more cheaply than blanket planting (Toh et al. 1999).
- In woodland, scattered trees concentrate nutrients and litter beneath their canopies and shelter the seedbed, doubling as nurse sites for the next cohort (Prober & Thiele 2005; Manning, Fischer & Lindenmayer 2006).

#### Deadwood feeding the trees: nutrient cycling and soil building

- Coarse woody debris holds a large reserve of nutrients and organic carbon and releases it slowly as it decays, so it sustains site productivity and soil organic carbon rather than letting nutrients leach away (Killey, McElhinny, Rayner & Wood 2010).
- Decaying wood intercepts mobilised soil particles and organic litter, reducing erosion and the loss of resources from a site (Killey et al. 2010).
- Across 66 studies (5,234 observations) adding woody debris raised soil function ~31 per cent, biota abundance ~156 per cent, and diversity ~106 per cent over debris-free soil, driven by the nutrient pulse of decay (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026).
- Decay releases staggered pulses: nitrogen availability rises as lignin breaks down and nitrogen-fixing bacteria colonise the wood, and calcium rises, while potassium leaches early, so a log feeds the soil different nutrients at different stages (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026; Laiho & Prescott 2004).
- Soil beside coarse woody debris in degraded eucalypt woodland is significantly higher in carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and nitrate, so a fallen log builds a fertile patch around itself (Goldin & Hutchinson 2013); in semi-arid mulga, contour-stacked branch piles trapped soil, water, and litter and raised soil nitrogen, carbon, infiltration, respiration, and fauna from bare ground (Tongway & Ludwig 1996).

#### Deadwood as seedbed and nurse log

- Seedlings establish and survive better on fallen wood than on bare, compacted, or erosion-prone ground: tree seedlings were significantly denser on fallen logs than adjacent soil in Tasmanian forest, with reduced litter cover, more moss, and lower bulk density the likely drivers (McKenny & Kirkpatrick 1999; Killey et al. 2010).
- Decaying wood holds moisture: surface soil beside coarse woody debris in cleared eucalypt woodland dried about 40 per cent more slowly than away from it, buffering the dry microsites where seedlings otherwise fail (Goldin & Hutchinson 2014).
- Woody debris also buffers temperature and moisture extremes and captures seed, generating distinct plant communities around it, and acts as a nursery for litter accumulation and fungal growth a cleared stand loses for decades (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026; Manning, Cunningham & Lindenmayer 2013).

#### Size, decay class, and benchmark loads

- Larger and older pieces do more: diversity rose ~15 per cent and abundance ~15 per cent per extra 10 cm of debris diameter and abundance ~14 per cent per decade on the ground, because large pieces hold distinct bark, sapwood, and heartwood substrates and pass through a long decomposer succession (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026).
- Large senescing trees supply most of the wood: a 100 cm diameter tree is ~10 times more likely to produce fallen debris than a 50 cm tree and produces ~10 times the volume, a Yellow Box can take over 200 years to reach that size, and one fallen bole 1 m across and 10 m long holds ~10 m3 of coarse woody debris (Killey et al. 2010).
- Benchmark fallen-branch loads for temperate Yellow Box and Red Gum woodland modelled at ~7.0 to 11.9 m3/ha, driven by large senescing trees (Killey et al. 2010); Australian forest-floor CWD ranges ~19 t/ha in woodland to ~134 t/ha in tall eucalypt forest, and eucalypt wood decays slowly (95 per cent decomposition takes ~7 years for *E. regnans* but up to ~375 years for *E. camaldulensis*), so large logs persist and feed the soil for centuries (Woldendorp & Keenan 2005).
- On south-eastern Australian River Red Gum floodplains current CWD averages ~19 t/ha, only ~15 per cent of an estimated pre-European ~125 t/ha, and full restoration would need the fallen-wood equivalent of ~3.3 to 3.4 million large River Red Gums (Mac Nally et al. 2002).

#### Urban deadwood retention and translocation

- Lightly managed urban stands can be deadwood refugia: random urban forest held a median ~10.1 m3/ha dead wood and high-value urban stands ~88.2 m3/ha (approaching semi-natural forest), so the practical lever is simply to leave more fallen or cut trees in place (Korhonen et al. 2020).
- Retaining natural deadwood is the priority because added debris does not fully reproduce natural wood fall, and managers should favour the large pieces that persist, since deadwood is routinely lost to firewood, access, and perceived fire risk (Mallen-Cooper et al. 2026).
- Where stands cannot yet supply their own wood, translocation and accelerated formation bridge the centuries-long gap: 2,000 tonnes of coarse woody debris sourced from removed Canberra street-tree eucalypts raised reptile abundance within four years, using large logs to mimic the slowest-forming debris (Manning, Cunningham & Lindenmayer 2013); translocating large deadwood to a compensation site rebuilt loads to ~20 m3/ha, the threshold for high saproxylic richness, a principle the authors extend to urban and infrastructure development (Tranberg et al. 2024).
- Translocation adds deadwood without felling living trees, so those trees mature and supply higher-quality wood later, and where old trees cannot be moved, veteranisation such as bark stripping accelerates deadwood and microhabitat formation in place (Tranberg et al. 2024).

#### Litter and self-mulching (the tree feeding its own root zone)

- Raking away a tree's own leaf litter cut soil decomposition 17 per cent and soil carbon up to 24 per cent, a legacy effect that re-retaining leaves did not reverse in 1-2 years (Ferlauto, Schmitt & Burghardt 2024); a large eucalypt drops ~10 times more litter under its crown than adjacent grass (12.5 vs 1.27 t/ha), building a fertile nutrient island around its own trunk (McElhinny et al. 2009).

#### Best examples

- The "living dead" woodland that self-recruits once we stop fertilising it: across 800,000 ha, removing superphosphate and switching to fast-rotational grazing lifted regeneration ~4-fold, best on poor soils (Fischer et al. 2009).
- River Red Gum seeding even-aged strips along a receding flood, then needing flooding roughly every three years to persist, so delivering environmental water is itself the recruitment intervention (Di Stefano 2002; Catelotti et al. 2015).
- A felled Canberra street-tree's afterlife: 2,000 t of its eucalypt wood, laid down as logs, raised reptile abundance within four years where decay alone would have taken a century (Manning, Cunningham & Lindenmayer 2013).
- The floodplain's missing forest of fallen wood: today's ~19 t/ha is ~15 per cent of the pre-European ~125 t/ha, a deficit equal to the fallen wood of ~3.3 million large River Red Gums (Mac Nally et al. 2002).

## Non-native tree value + non-native fungal connections in cities


### Mycorrhizal networks and soil biology in cities

- **What networks do**: shared fungal mycelium links trees and carries carbon, water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and defence signals along source-sink gradients; in old-growth Douglas-fir, single *Rhizopogon* genets linked up to 19 trees, with the largest and oldest trees the most-connected hubs.[^gorzelak2015][^beiler2010] Mycorrhizal fungi are up to a third of soil microbial biomass and supply up to 80 per cent of a tree's nitrogen.[^stevenson2020] Evidence status: transfer occurs, magnitude contested.
- **Inoculation is unreliable**: applying inoculum has not always led to significant differences; soil-injected *Pisolithus* on established street trees gave no growth benefit without fertiliser, and across 28 commercial inoculants on three continents, 84 per cent produced no colonisation in sterile soil and benefit appeared in just 1 of 25 non-sterile treatments. Urban soils are often already colonised by competitive native fungi, so inoculum is rarely the limiting factor. Evidence status: emerging and largely negative.
- **What does work**: keep legacy and veteran trees and their soil as living inoculum; clearcutting cut ectomycorrhizal refuge cover from 80 to 5 per cent in a year, and seedling colonisation was highest within 5 m of a retained tree. Soil decompaction, woodchip mulch, biochar and compost can rebuild fungal habitat; in Melbourne, biochar and compost each improved soil properties and *Corymbia maculata* growth, with no combined synergy.[^sommerville2020] Evidence status: established.
- **The critique to cite carefully**: Karst, Jones and Hoeksema reviewed 26 field studies and found three popular claims overstated: that networks are widespread, that resource transfer boosts seedling performance, and that mother trees preferentially feed offspring. They do not deny that networks exist. Carbon transfer is real but usually small relative to a tree's own photosynthesis. Use cautious, non-anthropomorphic framing.[^karst2023][^henriksson2023]
- **Urban conditions suppress the connections**: sealing, compaction, salt, and pollution reduce mycorrhizal colonisation, so urban trees host networks at lower levels than rural ones (Stevenson et al. 2020; UFUG 2023).
- **Best examples**: the 19-tree *Rhizopogon* map; "keep the elders, keep the network" (80 per cent to 5 per cent); rebuild soil to gain up to 84 per cent more canopy; buyer-beware evidence on bottled fungi (84 per cent failure).
- **Gap**: few field trials on broadleaf street trees; almost none measure network re-formation after urban soil rehab.

**References**: Gorzelak et al. 2015 (AoB Plants 7:plv050); Beiler et al. 2010 (New Phytologist 185:543); Karst, Jones & Hoeksema 2023 (Nat Ecol Evol 7:501); Klein et al. 2024 (response); Koziol et al. 2025 (New Phytologist); Smith / A&UF 2003 (29:107); Simard et al. 2020 (Frontiers Forests & Global Change 3:620436); Sommerville, Farrell, May & Livesley 2020 (Sci Total Environ 706:135736); Layman et al. 2016; Stevenson et al. 2020; Jim 2023 (Urban Ecosystems, rootability/soil husbandry).

### Value of exotics (and where natives still win)

- **The case for value**: non-natives can hold conservation value as habitat/food for rare species, functional substitutes, and ecosystem-function providers, and may gain value under future climate (Schlaepfer, Sax & Olden 2011; Schlaepfer 2018). Novel urban ecosystems can be better adapted to novel conditions, and introduced species are often "passengers rather than drivers" of native decline (Kowarik 2011). Reconciliation ecology: conserve biodiversity in altered habitats, not only reserves (Rosenzweig 2003; Lundholm & Richardson 2010).
- **Food and habitat resources**: exotic urban trees supply heavy floral resources (a single *Acer rubrum* ~1,350 flowers/m3, *Tilia* up to 2,400/m2) (Somme et al. 2016), and exotic oak/sycamore sustained native birds year-round (Gray & Van Heezik 2016). Sheffield's exotic-dominated gardens held >900 native invertebrate species/ha (Hitchmough 2011).
- **Honest counter-evidence (natives outperform for native fauna)**: UK native oak supported up to 286 insect species, non-native plane just 1 (Southwood 1961); a 70% native-biomass threshold was needed to sustain the insectivorous Carolina chickadee (Narango, Tallamy & Marra 2018); +30% native street trees gave +11% bird species in Canberra (Ikin et al. 2013); introduced hedgerows held 96% less caterpillar biomass (Richard, Tallamy & Mitchell 2019). The doc's existing line (natives are the better default, exotics still worth retaining) is well supported.

### Non-native fungal connections in cities

- **Urban ECM networks**: exotic ectomycorrhizal trees do form networks in cities, but urban ECM diversity is impoverished (sealing blocks dispersal, salt, low organic matter, buried pipes "in spatial conflict" with ECM networks); colonisation rates can still match forests (Authier, Violle & Richard 2022). Their design brief is "soil corridors for underground cities": interconnected planted pits and native-fungus inoculation, favouring high-connectivity hub hosts (oaks, beeches). Evidence status: emerging.
- **Pine co-invasion**: introduced pines are usually incompatible with local fungi and rely on co-introduced suilloids (*Suillus*, *Rhizopogon*); a single ECM fungus can enable a pine invasion, and lack of mutualists stalls it (Hayward et al. 2015; Nuñez, Horton & Simberloff 2009). Co-introduced communities are depauperate (often <20, sometimes 1-4 species, vs 100+ at home).
- **Eucalypts plug into native fungi**: planted *Eucalyptus globulus* in NW Spain associated with 26 ECM taxa, only 3 co-introduced Australian aliens, the majority novel partnerships with local fungi, with highest colonisation inside native oak forest (Santolamazza-Carbone et al. 2019) — but the co-introduced *Descolea maculata* then colonised native plants (a fungal co-invasion risk).
- **Best examples**: Californian urban butterflies now dependent on exotic larval plants (Shapiro 2002); the oak that is both fungal hub and faunal champion (286 insects vs the plane's 1); the pine paradox (invades only with its suilloid entourage); "soil corridors" written from the fungi's needs.
- **Gap**: native-fauna-use-of-exotic-street-trees data are thin for Melbourne specifically; no study measures functional ECM networks of exotic urban trees in Australian soils.

**References**: Schlaepfer, Sax & Olden 2011 (Conservation Biology 25:428); Schlaepfer 2018 (PLoS Biology 16:e2005046); Kowarik 2011 (Environmental Pollution 159:1974); Rosenzweig 2003; Lundholm & Richardson 2010 (J Applied Ecology 47:966); Somme et al. 2016 (Urban Ecosystems 19:1149); Gray & Van Heezik 2016 (Urban Ecosystems 19:315); Hitchmough 2011 (LUP 100:380); Liu & Slik 2022 (LUP 218:104304); Southwood 1961; Narango, Tallamy & Marra 2018 (PNAS 115:11549); Ikin et al. 2013; Richard, Tallamy & Mitchell 2019; Authier, Violle & Richard 2022 (Frontiers Plant Science 13:900231); Hayward et al. 2015 (Ecology 96:1438); Nuñez, Horton & Simberloff 2009 (Ecology 90:2352); Dickie et al. 2017 (AoB Plants 9:plw084); Santolamazza-Carbone, Durán-Otero & Calviño-Cancela 2019 (Scientific Reports 9:5868).


## Interventions to create a unified fungal network in urban conditions

**On the named article**: Harden and Moreno-Mateos do not show that a unified urban Common Mycorrhizal Network already exists. They propose an urban design hypothesis: if cities redesign soil, paving, planting composition, and underground infrastructure, then street trees, tree pits, planters, parks, and groves may become connected fungal habitat rather than isolated planting cells.[^harden2026] In this section, "unified fungal network" should therefore mean a designed, testable mosaic of connected fungal conditions, not a single seamless "wood-wide web" across the city.

### What a unified network can and cannot mean

- **Network transfer is possible, but contested in scale**: mycorrhizal mycelia can link plants and carry nutrients, water, carbon, defence signals, and allelochemicals, but the strength, ubiquity, and ecological importance of these transfers remain debated (Gorzelak et al. 2015; Klein et al. 2023; Karst, Jones & Hoeksema 2023).
- **Carbon transfer is not the whole story**: plants may route a large share of fixed carbon to fungal partners, and inter-tree carbon transfer has been measured, but Klein et al. frame the effect as real and modest, not a substitute for a tree's own photosynthesis.
- **Urban CMNs are less proven than forest CMNs**: Harden and Moreno-Mateos repeatedly frame urban mycorrhizal connectivity as underexplored. The design claim is therefore not "networks will communicate for us", but "soil, plants, and infrastructure can be arranged so fungal connection has a chance to form and can be measured."
- **AM and ECM fungi do not automatically merge**: arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) and ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungi are mostly distinct guilds. A unified urban system must work through compatible patches and interface species, not by assuming every tree can plug into every other tree (Stevenson et al. 2020; Teste, Jones & Dickie 2020; Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026).

### 1. Create fungal-ready ground before adding fungi

- **Soil volume and rootable space first**: suspended pavements, structural cells, root paths, trenches, and structured soils create the physical space for roots. Harden and Moreno-Mateos treat root expansion as the precondition for mycelial colonisation and tree-to-tree connectivity.[^harden2026]
- **Permeability plus organic matter**: permeable asphalt, concrete grids, and pavers can deliver water and oxygen to the root-fungal zone, but they can also stop leaf litter and plant debris from reaching detritivorous fungi. The intervention is therefore permeability plus mulch, litter return, compost, deadwood, or other organic inputs, not permeability alone.[^harden2026]
- **Soil chemistry and stress filters**: salinity, heavy metals, altered pH, low organic matter, and compaction can suppress colonisation or shift fungal communities. Fungal-network design therefore belongs with decompaction, stormwater infiltration, organic-matter return, and contamination management, not only with planting layout (Stevenson et al. 2020; Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026).

### 2. Link isolated planting cells with soil conduits

- **Infrastructure as underground crossing**: Harden and Moreno-Mateos explicitly model soil conduits on wildlife overpasses and pollinator corridors. The conduit is an urban infrastructure device that lets roots and mycelium cross the hard city matrix between tree pits, street trees, planters, parks, and groves.[^harden2026]
- **Material form**: the proposed conduit is an open-air trench or root-path system with horticultural soil, organic mulch, a grate for air and pedestrian passage, drainage material below, and enough depth and width to support roots and fungal growth. The review's prototype details include about 30 cm of mulch-covered soil, crushed-stone drainage, and a narrow linear path sized to fit between street trees.[^harden2026]
- **Design questions**: the conduit is not yet a proven technology. Open questions include how many conduits are needed, how long and wide they must be, whether they should carry the same or different mycorrhizal types as adjacent plants, and whether connected soils actually develop higher inoculum potential than unconnected soils.[^harden2026]

### 3. Organise plantings by mycorrhizal compatibility

- **Same-guild patches**: AM-associated trees and understorey plants can be grouped to reinforce AM networks; ECM-associated trees and shrubs can be grouped to reinforce ECM networks. Harden and Moreno-Mateos give AM overstorey-understorey examples and separate ECM configurations, then link patches through conduits.[^harden2026]
- **Species selection as fungal infrastructure**: tree choice is not only canopy, shade, drought tolerance, or heritage. It also decides which fungal guild can plausibly form belowground. Eucalypts, oaks, pines, willows, and poplars are ECM or dual; many other urban trees are AM (Teste, Jones & Dickie 2020; Shi et al. 2023).
- **Avoid false universality**: an AM avenue, an ECM grove, and a mixed urban park may each support fungal life, but they are not automatically one compatible network. The planting plan has to specify where same-guild reinforcement is intended and where cross-guild interfaces are being tested.

### 4. Bridge incompatible fungal types with dual-mycorrhizal plants

- **Bridge plants, not magic converters**: the "converter" idea is useful if framed as an interface. Dual-mycorrhizal plants can associate with both AM and ECM fungi, so they may help expand or connect fungal-network patches that would otherwise remain guild-specific.[^harden2026]
- **Candidate bridge genera**: Harden and Moreno-Mateos, drawing on Teste et al., list *Acacia*, *Alnus*, *Eucalyptus*, *Fraxinus*, *Populus*, *Salix*, *Shorea*, and *Uapaca* as dual-mycorrhizal plant groups. For Melbourne, *Eucalyptus* and *Acacia* are especially important because they can be both indigenous habitat trees and possible fungal interface plants.[^harden2026]
- **Unified network as mosaic**: the practical target is a linked mosaic: AM patches, ECM patches, dual-mycorrhizal interface plants, and soil conduits that physically join them. This is stronger than isolated tree pits, but still more honest than claiming one universal fungal web.

### 5. Use inoculation as a monitored support, not a shortcut

- **Compatibility controls success**: inoculation may improve drought tolerance, disease resistance, and plant physiology, but successful inoculation depends on matching host plant, fungal species, soil conditions, and existing indigenous inoculum potential.[^harden2026]
- **Commercial inoculants are risky evidence**: the review notes little-to-no effect, antagonism with fertiliser, ineffective commercial products compared with rural forest soil, and possible harms from invasive isolates, pathogens, or competition with resident fungi.[^harden2026]
- **Melbourne eucalypt complication**: much of the ECM diversity supporting eucalypts is hypogeous and animal-dispersed. Potoroos and bettongs disperse viable spores through digging and dung; Tasmanian bettong digging rose up to ten-fold after fire; and ECM has been raised on Eucalyptus roots from potoroo dung (Maser, Claridge & Trappe 2008; Claridge 1994; Johnson 1995). In the urban matrix, those animal-fungal pathways are largely absent, so inoculation or donor-soil work may be replacing a missing animal relation, not simply adding a product.

### Design implications for keeping urban trees fungally connected

- Retain legacy and large old trees as living fungal reservoirs and the most plausible local inoculum source for nearby plantings (Beiler et al. 2010; Stevenson et al. 2020).
- Rehabilitate soil rather than sterilise it: decompaction plus organic matter raised canopy and sped establishment over six years (Layman et al. 2016).
- Preserve soil continuity, avoid wholesale soil stripping at planting, feed soil biota with mulch, compost, biochar, litter, and deadwood, and design belowground conduits rather than isolated pits (Robertson 2020; Turner et al. 2025; Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026).
- Pair material continuity with biological compatibility: plant AM and ECM patches deliberately, then use dual-mycorrhizal species as possible bridge plants where fungal guilds meet (Teste et al. 2020; Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026).
- Treat fungal-network infrastructure as a trial: compare connected and unconnected soils for inoculum potential, fungal colonisation, tree stress, water status, soil organic matter, pathogen risk, and evidence of functional plant-fungal exchange.[^harden2026]
- **Caveat for the paper**: donor-soil, inoculation, bridge-planting, and soil-conduit interventions are biologically reasonable but the urban evidence base is thin and outcomes inconsistent, so present them as promising and testable, not proven (Stevenson et al. 2020; Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026). Evidence status: emerging/speculative.

### Best examples

- Soil conduits as underground wildlife crossings: street-tree pits become less like pots and more like patches joined by belowground corridors, a direct translation of animal bridge logic into fungal infrastructure (Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026).
- Bridge planting as fungal interface: *Eucalyptus* and *Acacia* can be read as possible AM/ECM interface plants, not just as canopy or understorey species, because they may help connect otherwise incompatible fungal guilds (Teste et al. 2020; Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026).
- A bettong's nose as a forester's tool: post-fire, Tasmanian bettong digging for underground truffles jumped up to tenfold within a month, pulse-dispersing the ectomycorrhizal fungi eucalypts regenerate with, a tight animal-fungus-fire-tree loop almost entirely missing from city soils (Johnson 1995).
- Inoculation by faeces: ectomycorrhizas have been raised on Eucalyptus roots directly from long-nosed potoroo dung, the clearest sign that a marsupial's gut is part of the eucalypt's root system (Maser, Claridge & Trappe 2008).
- Mycorrhiza as feminist figure: an interview frames María Lugones's anti-purity relational philosophy through mycelial networks, exactly the porous, connected-being move the persona paper can lean on (Veronelli & Zurn 2025).

**References**: Harden and Moreno-Mateos 2026 (Ecological Restoration 44:23); Gorzelak et al. 2015 (AoB Plants 7:plv050); Klein, Rog, Livne-Luzon, van der Heijden & Körner 2023 (Open Research Europe 3:168); Karst, Jones & Hoeksema 2023 (Nature Ecology & Evolution 7:501); Henriksson et al. 2023 (New Phytologist 239:19); Stevenson et al. 2020 (Plants People Planet 2:482); Teste, Jones & Dickie 2020 (New Phytologist 225:1835); Shi, Wang & Wang 2023 (Annual Review of Plant Biology 74); Maser, Claridge & Trappe 2008 (*Trees, Truffles, and Beasts*, Rutgers UP); Claridge et al. 1994 (Australian Journal of Ecology 19); Johnson 1995 (Oecologia 104:467); Beiler et al. 2010 (New Phytologist 185:543); Sheldrake 2020 (*Entangled Life*); Tsing 2011 (Australian Humanities Review 50 / MUSE 407437) & 2015 (*The Mushroom at the End of the World*); Barnett 2023 (Journal of Ecohumanism 2:1); DeFalco 2024 (*Palgrave Handbook of Literature and Aging*); Veronelli & Zurn 2025 (philoSOPHIA 15:61); Cavanagh 2020 (The Conversation); Pouliot 2018 (*The Allure of Fungi*, CSIRO); Robertson 2020 (Australian Geographer 51:4); Turner, Hill & Abramovic 2025 (Local Environment 30); Layman et al. 2016 (UFUG 16:25).

**Gap**: Harden and Moreno-Mateos frame soil conduits and bridge-planting as design hypotheses requiring systematic testing; no Melbourne-specific study of urban-eucalypt mycorrhizal status, conduit performance, or inoculation outcome exists, so the urban-disconnection claim is a reasoned inference.
